transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-17 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48m
Attendees: Maya Chen, Omar Nazir, Lina Gómez (Redwood); Rachel Kim, Tomás Villanueva, Priya Singh, Alex Green (Argentum)

[00:00] Maya: Hi everyone, thanks for carving the time. Quick intros?
[00:12] Rachel: Rachel — Head of ML at Argentum, we own the underwriting models and the decisions flow.
[00:18] Tomás: Tomás, infra lead, ops and cost owner.
[00:24] Priya: Priya, product, driving timeline — want this in pilot by end of Q1.
[00:29] Alex: Alex, security. I have a few compliance questions.
[00:33] Maya: Great. Omar and Lina here on the technical side. Today's goal: map unit economics for your usage patterns and surface tradeoffs between hosted, dedicated, and private. Also cover batching, KV/prefix cache, and fallback behavior.

[03:05] Omar: Can you share an expected qps and payload distribution? That drives batching efficiency.
[03:14] Tomás: Sure — right now we're prototyping with a 500 reqs/min workload during peak — median prompt length ~180 tokens, p95 around 620 tokens. Mostly short form responses for loan decisioning though some followups get longer.
[03:40] Lina: Okay that’s useful. Two levers: batching (grouping concurrent requests) and KV / prefix caching for repeated prefixes will cut per-token compute. For dedicated, you can get consistent throughput and we can tune batching windows. For hosted, we do more autoscaling and intelligent routing — cheaper to start.

[07:02] Priya: Real question: what's the delta per-token cost hosted vs dedicated, ignoring committed discounts?
[07:12] Maya: Short answer — hosted list is higher per-token but zero infra ops. Dedicated with a medium reserved footprint can cut unit cost 30–45% depending on utilization and batching. We'll model your exact numbers in the spreadsheet.

[09:45] Rachel: But latency matters — we can't add 200ms for batching if it affects user flow. How does Redwood trade latency for batch size?
[09:59] Omar: We do continuous batching with micro-batch windows — typically 10–40ms for strict latency SLOs. For higher throughput routes you can tolerate 50–200ms windows to get larger batch sizes. Also prefix/KV cache hits are served from cache and avoid recomputation expensive tokens. But cache hit rate depends on prompt template reuse.

[12:20] Tomás: What's realistic cache hit rate for decisioning prompts? We reuse a lot of templated preamble and risk-scorer calls, so maybe 30–60%?
[12:30] Lina: If templates are consistent and you normalize inputs, hitting 40% cache is reasonable; aggressive normalization plus token bucketing can push higher.

[14:15] Priya: On the security front — we need SOC2, KMS integration, and maybe a VPC/private option. If we go private, how does that affect cost?
[14:32] Maya: Private deployments (VPC or on-prem) come with platform fees and higher ops costs — typically add 20–60% overhead to the baseline serving cost because of dedicated control plane, networking, and support SLAs. But they give residency and isolation required for regulated data.

[16:48] Alex: Encryption: do you integrate with customer KMS or HSM? We need control of keys at rest, and audit logs.
[16:58] Lina: Yes, private and dedicated both support customer-managed KMS integration and audit exports. Hosted supports envelope encryption and Redwood-managed keys, and we can scope KMS bring-your-own for hosted enterprise tiers.

[19:10] Rachel: For the pilot we want to baseline two configs: hosted (fast go) and dedicated small pool (to see cost/latency delta). What metrics should we collect?
[19:22] Omar: Request-level token counts, per-token latency contribution, batch size distribution, cache hit rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, and cost per token estimate. Also tail latencies during bursts.

[21:48] Tomás: How do fallbacks work — if dedicated pool is saturated?
[21:55] Maya: We offer routing policies. For dedicated you can set preferred pools then fallback to hosted model variants or smaller capacity instances. Fallbacks ensure availability but you should expect some delta in model variant (e.g., quantized variant) and modest increase in latency. We'll show a routing policy example in the pilot plan.

[24:30] Priya: We're sensitive about hallucinations for decisions. If we quantize aggressively to save cost, will output quality degrade?
[24:40] Lina: Quantization can affect quality depending on model and quant format. Our Optimize toolkit recommends quantization profiles per workload and runs regression checks against your eval set. For high-stakes outputs we recommend lighter quantization or keeping critical routes on higher precision variants.

[27:05] Rachel: Budget constraint — we have a token budget cap for pilot of roughly $8k/month. How can we structure traffic to fit within that without losing SLOs?
[27:18] Omar: Options: 1) Use aggressive prefix caching and template normalization to reduce redundant token generation. 2) Slice usage: route low-risk, high-volume calls to quantized variants or batched paths, keep latency-critical calls on high-precision variants. 3) Use rate-based throttling and prioritized queues. We'll model scenarios in the pricing spreadsheet.

[30:40] Tomás: Can you share an example worksheet row for a 1M token month and how batching affects the cost?
[30:48] Maya: We'll include a worked example: baseline per-token hosted price, then savings from batching at different concurrency shapes, and cache-hit delta. Also show TCO for dedicated with a 3–6 month commit.

[33:20] Alex: On compliance docs — can you provide SOC2 report and network diagrams for hosted?
[33:27] Lina: Yes, we have a SOC2 summary and can provide redacted diagrams and a data flow doc. For private we give full on-prem docs. We'll send links in the followup.

[36:05] Priya: Timeline — pilot by end of Q1. We need to know how long Dedicated provisioning takes if we want to try it after pilot.
[36:16] Maya: Dedicated racks typically 4–8 weeks to provision and test; private longer depending on on-prem. Hosted pilot can start within days after sharing traffic shapes and credentials for test harness.

[38:50] Tomás: For the benchmark run, what do you need from our side?
[38:57] Omar: Sample prompt set, traffic replay or synthetic trace, SLO target definitions, and a contact for infra to coordinate IP allowlist or VPC peering for the test.

[41:22] Rachel: If we hit cost overages during pilot, how do charges work and are there protective caps?
[41:31] Maya: We can set hard budget caps on hosted, and alerts for projected burn rates. For pilots we often set a cap and pause behavior, plus detailed cost reports.

[43:05] Priya: Anything else around operational playbooks?
[43:12] Lina: We'll provide runbooks for failover and routing policies, and a recommended rollout: start hosted -> pilot measurement -> evaluate dedicated for steady-state with 1–3 months commit if consistent.

[46:00] Maya: Recap: Redwood to send pilot pricing spreadsheet + worked examples, pilot test plan, SOC2 and KMS docs links; Argentum to share token distribution and canonical prompts and pick pilot dates.
[46:25] Rachel: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[46:30] Maya: I'll follow up with the links and proposed dates by Thursday.
[46:36] [meeting end]
